Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does:
  - It first creates a MultiValueMap using a safe collection class (ArrayList.class), serializes it, and deserializes it. This should succeed.
  - It then creates another MultiValueMap using a deliberately unsafe class via a raw cast: MultiValueMap.multiValueMap(new HashMap(), (Class) String.class). It serializes that and then attempts to deserialize it. The test expects deserialization to be rejected with an UnsupportedOperationException. Instead, deserialization succeeds, causing the test to fail.

- Relevant code paths:
  - MultiValueMap.multiValueMap(Map, Class):
    - Returns new MultiValueMap<>(map, new ReflectionFactory<>(collectionClass)) (lines 104–107).
  - MultiValueMap(Map, Factory):
    - The constructor stores the provided factory in this.collectionFactory without validating it (lines 144–152).
  - MultiValueMap():
    - Defaults to ReflectionFactory(ArrayList.class), which is safe (lines 131–134).
  - Factory.create():
    - The factory is an abstraction for creating instances; ReflectionFactory implements this and will attempt to instantiate the provided Class via reflection.

- How the bug manifests:
  - The constructor MultiValueMap(map, Factory) accepts any Factory without runtime validation of the type of collection it will produce.
  - multiValueMap(map, Class) wraps the provided Class in a ReflectionFactory. While generics constrain C extends Collection<V> at compile time, the test uses a raw cast to bypass generics and supplies String.class.
  - On serialization, MultiValueMap persists its collectionFactory (which is a ReflectionFactory with String.class).
  - On deserialization, there is no guard in MultiValueMap to validate that the deserialized factory will create a type that actually implements java.util.Collection. As a result, the object is accepted, and no exception is thrown.
  - Therefore, deserializing the bytes of a MultiValueMap constructed with String.class succeeds, violating the safety expectation and causing the test to fail with “unsafe clazz accepted when de-serializing MultiValueMap”.

- Security context (from the issue report):
  - The broader vulnerability described involves gadget chains enabling arbitrary code execution upon deserialization. Accepting arbitrary factories/classes during deserialization (e.g., via a reflection-based factory) makes MultiValueMap a potential gadget because it can be crafted to instantiate or trigger code in classes with harmful constructors or side effects.
  - The test enforces a safety barrier: deserialization must reject MultiValueMap instances whose collectionFactory would not create a legitimate Collection, preventing misuse and reducing gadget potential.

- Root cause:
  - Missing validation in MultiValueMap’s deserialization path: it does not verify that the deserialized collectionFactory is safe (i.e., it will create a type that implements java.util.Collection). Consequently, an unsafe class (String.class in the test) is accepted when deserializing, instead of throwing UnsupportedOperationException as required by the test and the security hardening goals.

- Why the first part of the test passes:
  - When using ArrayList.class, the ReflectionFactory targets a class that is a legitimate Collection. Even without validation, deserialization is safe and should not throw, so the first deserialization completes successfully.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
